title: Token lifecycle attribution runbook and low-fidelity prototypes
content:
Purpose and quick context:
This doc captures framing, low-fidelity wire ideas, interaction patterns, and a prioritized grooming backlog for a Token Lifecycle Attribution view. Goal is to give product + infra + SRE teams a lightweight, interactive way to reconcile per-invocation cost and latency spikes down to token-level events (batching, prefix cache hits, model fallback, kernel switch, tokenization differences). This is a companion to the existing cost + latency surfaces; it should focus on attribution, playback, and actionability rather than raw aggregation.

Audience / personas:
- Platform engineer diagnosing a 99th percentile latency regression across a route. Needs to know whether batching or KV-cache misses caused the spike and whether a model fallback triggered downstream cost increases.
- App engineer investigating hallucination/cost anomalies for a user-facing workflow; wants to replay the invocation and inspect which tokens drove the delta.
- Product manager wanting to group invocations by behavior and tag representative traces for evals.

Success criteria (how we will judge this feature):
- Time-to-root-cause: reduce median time engineers spend from alert -> plausible root cause by 40% in lab tasks.
- Actionability: at least three remediation actions surfaced (pin model variant, change batching policy, prewarm KV cache) with clear button-driven next steps.
- Low cognitive load: new users can use core playback + attribution features in <= 3 minutes after onboarding.

High-level interaction model (happy path):
1) User sees an invocation list filtered by route/time; selects a single invocation.
2) Top-level summary: invocation-level cost, latency, model variant, region, queue time.
3) Below: a synchronized timeline/waterfall: left side is the invocation timeline (request -> queue -> model stages -> token emission), right side is token waterfall with two stacked bars per token: latency contribution (ms) and cost contribution ($-scaled).
4) Play/Pause + Scrubber: user can play tokens in emission order; scrubber shows current token, streaming token text, and side-by-side diff of inference time and cost vs baseline (baseline = chosen reference invocation or model default).
5) Attribution overlays: toggle overlays for batching boundaries, prefix-cache hit/miss, fallback events, quantization/precision mode, and kernel selection. Hovering a token shows metadata: token id, byte size, tokenization boundary, KV-cache status, assigned batch id, latency histogram snippet, and associated GPU kernel.

Wireframe notes (low-fi, for engineering to implement quickly):
- Header: single-line metadata chips (model, variant, route, region, invocation-id, commit). Quick action buttons: pin-as-reference, add-to-eval, open-runbook.
- Left column (0.35 width): timeline swimlane. Rows: client -> load-balancer -> preprocessor -> router -> queue -> serving nodes. Events are compact rectangles; clicking expands event to show logs and traces.
- Middle column (0.4 width): token waterfall. Each token rendered as stacked thin bars: dark = compute latency, light = scheduling/queue latency, outline = cost proxy. Vertical grouping marks batches.
- Right column (0.25 width): token inspector panel with two tabs: "Token detail" and "Attribution trace". Token detail shows text, tokenizer offsets, source (prefix vs user), embeddings cost, and small sparkline of latency across N recent invocations. Attribution trace shows inferred cause chain for the current token (e.g., batch boundary -> KV miss -> fallback to fp16 -> extra decoding tokens).
- Playback controls pinned to footer: speed control (0.25x, 1x, 2x), scrub drag, step-forward/back by token, step-by-edge-of-batch.

Unique UX affordances (these differ from other dashboards):
- Emission-replay with token-level diff: instead of static bars only, animation highlights token-level differences between two invocations (A vs B) so users can see where costs diverge as tokens flow out.
- Batch-map heat overlay: a semi-transparent band behind tokens showing batch size when each token was served; useful to spot micro-batching boundaries that increase tail latency.
- Cost normalization toggle: switch between absolute dollars, cost per 1k tokens, and compute-time-proxy. Helpful to compare across model variants.
- Predicate-based slicing: quick filters like "first N tokens of streaming response", "tokens after fallback event", or arbitrary regex on token text to isolate suspicious tokens (e.g., repeated stop-word expansions).

Edge cases and constraints:
- Long invocations ( >10k tokens ) should be collapsed into ranges. Offer an aggregated super-token that expands on demand to avoid rendering/scroll costs.
- Streaming cases: ensure playback handles partial responses; scrub state should indicate which upstream chunks were missing and whether backpressure occurred.
- Privacy: tokens may contain PII. By default redact token text in shared/public views; show policy banner with buttons to reveal when authorized.

Backlog (prioritized, rough sizes):
1) Core timeline + token waterfall + playback scrubber (MVP) — 5 story points. Acceptance: select invocation -> play tokens -> see latency/cost bars + hover shows metadata.
2) Token inspector panel + overlays (batch, KV-hit/miss, fallback) — 3 pts. Acceptance: toggles reflect on waterfall and inspector shows correct KV status for hovered token.
3) Compare mode (A vs B emission diff) — 5 pts. Acceptance: user can pin ref invocation and see per-token delta animation.
4) Predicate slicing UI + regex filter + saved slices — 3 pts. Acceptance: create slice -> list filters invocations matching condition.
5) Cost normalization and export (CSV/JSON of tokens with attributions) — 2 pts.
6) Redaction/PII controls + audit log (enterprise) — 4 pts.
7) Accessibility pass (keyboard scrub, screen reader labels for tokens) — 2 pts.
8) Backfill demo dataset + product e2e test — 3 pts.

Open questions / discussion items (for next grooming):
- Baseline model for delta: should reference be the most recent successful invocation, the latest production commit, or a user-selected pinned reference? (tradeoffs in storage and UX).
- How to surface cost attribution for shared resources (e.g., batching that combines many invocations)? Proposed: attribute proportional cost to tokens by compute time weight; discussion needed with infra cost accounting.
- Should token-level exports include raw token text by default? Security/compliance implications.
- Can we reliably annotate kernel selection per token? Some kernel decisions occur per attention block not token; we should decide approximation strategy.

Notes to self / next steps before dev kickoff:
- Finalize data contract with Serving Runtime team: include token timestamps, batch_id, kv_hit boolean, kernel_tag, model_variant, and op-level timings.
- Create a small mock dataset (~200 invocations) that includes typical failure modes: batch-spike, kv-miss storm, fallback loop, quantization artifact. Use that for early demo.
- Draft short rubric for the usability lab that measures TTRC (time to root cause) and clarity of remediation path.
- Sync with security on PII redaction UI and enterprise audit events.

Quick sketch links (Figma): see linked artifacts.

Slack references / threads: #console-design thread 'token-attribution-mvp' (last message 2025-02-21) and reference to infra latency trace conversation (thread id in Jira-1254).

Appendix: example invocation narrative (for UX copy/testing)
- 11:43:07.123 - request accepted; route = /chat/assist-basic; model = open-mpt-11B-v2-q4; user prefix = 45 tokens; user prompt = 68 tokens.
- 11:43:07.150 - batched with 12 other invocations; batch_id = 0x3a7; predecode delay = 22 ms.
- 11:43:07.189 - KV-cache miss for prefix; fallback to disk prewarm (180 ms).
- 11:43:07.380 - model fallback detected to fp16 kernel for decoding (increases per-token latency by ~1.6x).
- 11:43:07.682 onward - streaming emits tokens; tokens 1..10 show small compute times, token 11 shows spike due to kernel switch and is highlighted in UI.

This narrative will be used in the demo dataset and as a guided tour script for the feature.

-- Ava N.
